prose.def: A prison or jail — a place where people are held in physical confinement under guard.
prose.article: δεσμωτήριον means a prison or jail, a place where people are held in bondage. It appears just 4 times in the New Testament, and the meaning is stable: every occurrence is rendered as 'prison' or 'jail.' The word is built from a root meaning 'to bind,' and it shows up in everyday Koine papyri, where documents speak of people being thrown into the local δεσμωτήριον — in the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew word for the prison where Joseph was held.
prose.caution: With only 4 occurrences, the evidence is thin, though the meaning is consistent across all sources.

audit.author_note: Matthew uses the word once for John the Baptist's imprisonment and Acts uses it three times for apostolic and civic detentions; the meaning is identical across both authors, with no detectable theological or semantic difference.

prose.def: A person physically restrained in bonds or under guard as a prisoner, unable to escape.
prose.article: δεσμώτης simply means a prisoner — someone held in bonds or custody. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in the same chapter (Acts 27:1 and 27:42), where it describes captives being transported by ship, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "prisoners" in 100% of cases. The word was at home in everyday Koine: a papyrus from 258 BC speaks of prisoners being delivered by an administrator named Apollonios and the need for more room to hold them.

prose.def: A master with full authority over slaves or a household; also a title for God or Christ as absolute Sovereign Lord.
prose.article: δεσπότης names someone with total ownership and uncontrolled power, the counterpart to a slave. In the New Testament it appears 10 times: about two-thirds (6×) refer to human masters of slaves, while a couple (2×) are addressed to God as "Lord." The everyday papyri confirm this hard sense of ownership — in one letter from 13 BC the writer is literally the slave's δεσπότης, and a related document speaks of legal "lordship" (δεσποτεία) over property. Lexicons note it implies absolute mastery, in contrast to κύριος, which suggests a more general or limited authority.

prose.def: An adverbial exclamation meaning 'come!' or 'come here!' used to summon someone, and in Paul (ROM 1:13) a temporal adverb meaning 'up to now' or 'hitherto.'
prose.article: At its core δεῦρο is a one-word command—"come!" or "come here!"—used with someone you're calling to yourself, as when Jesus says "come, follow Me" (Matthew 19:21) or calls out "Lazarus, come forth!" (John 11:43). In the Byzantine New Testament the MSB renders it "come" in 3 of 9 cases, while the other occurrences get folded into the surrounding phrasing. It also carries a temporal sense, "up to now," and the papyri nicely confirm this: documents from around A.D. 150–346 use phrases like "up to the present" (μέχρι τοῦ δεῦρο), strikingly close to Paul's own wording.
prose.caution: With only 9 occurrences and just 3 directly rendered "come," the measured data is thin, and the lexicons add a temporal sense ("now, hitherto") that the Byzantine count barely captures.

prose.def: An exclamatory call meaning 'Come!' or 'Come on!', used alone as a direct summons or paired with another verb to invite joint action.
prose.article: δεῦτε is an exclamatory call meaning "come!" or "come here!"—functioning like the plural of δεῦρο. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 13 times, rendered simply "Come" in 7 cases (58%) and "Come let" in 3 (25%), the latter when it pairs with another verb to summon people into joint action, as in the parable vineyard schemes (Matthew 21:38, Mark 12:7, Luke 20:14). It often combines with prepositions—"come after me" in Matthew 4:19, "come to me" in Matthew 11:28—and in the Septuagint, where it occurs 40 times, it chiefly renders the Hebrew imperative לְכוּ ("go!" or "come!").

prose.def: Describing something that happens on the second day after an event, often translated as an adverb like "on the next day."
prose.article: δευτεραῖος is an adjective formed from δεύτερος ("second") that functions like an English adverb, describing arrival or action "on the second day." It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 28:13, where the Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render it in connection with "second." The Greek construction is striking: it uses an adjective (literally "second-day men") where English naturally wants an adverb, so the KJV simply translates "the next day."
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single occurrence.

prose.def: A Greek term of uncertain meaning, traditionally taken as a label for a particular Sabbath, possibly the second after Passover.
prose.article: This is one of the most famously puzzling words in the New Testament, appearing just once across one book in the Byzantine text (Luke 6:1) and dropped entirely from the modern critical text. Its parts mean "second" and "first," and Strong's guesses it labels a specific Sabbath after Passover, but the dictionaries are blunt: Dodson calls it "a word of uncertain meaning" and Abbott-Smith says there is no satisfactory explanation. The most striking note comes from Moulton-Milligan, who searched the everyday papyri and found no support at all, calling it a famous "vox nihili" — a word that may not really be a word — whose only real interest is how it ever slipped into the text.
prose.caution: This is a single, textually disputed occurrence whose meaning no source can explain with confidence, and the modern critical text omits it entirely.

receipts.how: The sole Byzantine-text occurrence where δευτερόπρωτος appears as a modifier for σαββάτῳ, demonstrating both its unique attestation and its absorbed-into-phrasing syntactic role that defies clean translation.
Abbott-Smith's marginal note (WH mg., R mg.) confirms the word is textually disputed and absent from the critical text, supporting the definition's caution about uncertain meaning and textual status.
Moulton-Milligan's 'vox nihili' judgment, cited in the article, is anchored to this single verse and validates the definition's framing of the term as possibly not a genuine word at all.

prose.def: To receive or accept a person, thing, or message — whether by welcoming someone in person, accepting an object, or inwardly embracing a word or gift.
senseLabels: receive (embedded in relative clause, same sense as 1–2)
prose.article: At its core δέχομαι means to take what is offered—whether a person you welcome or a thing you accept. In the Byzantine New Testament's 58 occurrences, it splits mainly between "welcome" (20×, 43%) and "received" (17×, 36%), with many cases woven into phrases about receiving people in Jesus' name. The everyday flavor shows clearly in the papyri, where business receipts use it for acknowledging payment: "I have received from you the sum in full without any arrears."
prose.caution: The various "whoever"-type sense labels mostly reflect English phrasing of the same welcoming/receiving idea rather than truly distinct meanings.

prose.def: A small particle that sharpens or adds urgency to the word it modifies—commands, exhortations, or pronouns—roughly equivalent to 'now,' 'indeed,' or 'then.'

with indicative or other construction: emphasis or specification
prose.article: δή is a tiny particle with no exact English equivalent; it adds emphasis or exactness to whatever word it attaches to, often rendered "now," "then," "indeed," or left untranslated. It is rare in the New Testament, appearing only 7 times across 6 books, and it frequently attaches to commands and exhortations (as in "Let us go now"). It is far more common in the Septuagint, where it appears 274 times and overwhelmingly renders the Hebrew particle נָא (183×), a word that softens or urges a request. The everyday papyri show the same flavor, as in P Oxy 907's λέγω δὴ τῇ Διδύμῃ, "to wit, Didyme."
prose.caution: The measured "senses" here are really fragments of surrounding translation rather than distinct meanings, since this particle rarely maps to a single English word and is sometimes absorbed into phrasing entirely.

prose.def: Describing something plain, evident, or manifest — whether clearly recognizable in context or logically self-evident, sometimes used adverbially to mean 'certainly.'
prose.article: δῆλος means "clear" or "evident" — not visible to the eye so much as obvious to the understanding. It appears only 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament, often in the phrase "it is clear that" (as in 1 Corinthians 15:27 and Galatians 3:11). Abbott-Smith draws a nice contrast: φανερός means manifest to outward sight, while δῆλος means evident to inner perception; everyday Koine papyri confirm this, repeatedly using δῆλον for what is plainly so, like a petition stating that something "is forbidden by the law — that is clear." In the Septuagint it interestingly stands in for the Hebrew Urim (3×), the priestly objects used to make God's will known.
prose.caution: With only 4 occurrences and the measured renderings ("one," "put," "certainly") reflecting surrounding phrases rather than the word itself, the corpus data is thin and best read alongside the lexical sense "clear, evident."

prose.article: δηλόω means to make something plain to the mind—to inform, declare, or point out a meaning. Abbott-Smith notes a useful distinction from ἐμφανίζω: that word means to make visible to the sight, while δηλόω makes something evident to the mind.

prose.article: δημιουργός literally combines "people" (δῆμος) and "work" (ἔργον), originally meaning one who works for the public, and it broadened to mean a craftsman, builder, or maker. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 11:10, where it describes God as the builder of the city Abraham looked forward to. Abbott-Smith notes a subtle distinction in that verse: a related word (τεχνίτης) points to the plan, while δημιουργός points to carrying it out. The papyri show the word in everyday use and even in early Christian prayers, where God is called both "almighty" and δημιουργός.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured rendering "looking" reflects the surrounding verse rather than the word's actual meaning of "builder."

prose.def: The common people of a city, especially as a gathered crowd or formal civic assembly; in NT use often carrying the sense of a mere rabble rather than a sovereign demos.
prose.article: δῆμος refers to the ordinary people of a city viewed as a public body, often a crowd or popular assembly. It appears only 4 times in the New Testament, all in Acts, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "people" twice plus phrases tied to crowds and assemblies in the other two cases. Lexicographers distinguish it from related words: λαός tends to mean the people as a whole (often Israel), while δῆμος is the people as a body politic, and ὄχλος is an unorganized mob. Interestingly, in the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew מִשְׁפָּחָה ("clan, family") 136 times, and one scholar notes its New Testament uses suggest merely a rabble, since real Greek civic freedom had faded.
prose.caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the measured senses rest on thin data, and the breakdown into separate "senses" partly reflects differing translation phrasing rather than clearly distinct meanings.

prose.def: Belonging to the people or state (public); used as an adverb in the dative feminine to mean publicly, in the open — found only in Acts.
prose.article: δημόσιος describes something belonging to the people or the community — public property, public officials, or actions done in the open. In the New Testament it appears only 4 times, all in Acts, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "public" twice, "publicly" once, and as part of "anything helpful publicly" once; the feminine dative form works as an adverb meaning "in public." The papyri make the everyday flavor vivid: it was an extremely common label for public officials (δημόσιοι) and public taxes or roads (ὁδὸς δημοσία), showing it was ordinary civic vocabulary.
prose.caution: With only 4 occurrences and three closely related shades of meaning, the line between "public" and "publicly" depends on grammar more than a sharp difference in sense.

prose.def: A denarius, a Roman silver coin worth about a day's wages for a laborer.
prose.article: The δηνάριον was a Roman silver coin, borrowed into Greek straight from the Latin denarius, and the New Testament uses it 16 times simply to name that coin. The two measured senses are just grammatical number—singular "denarius" 9 times (56%) and plural "denarii" 7 times (44%)—so the meaning never really shifts. It was a common everyday unit: a papyrus receipt from A.D. 187 records someone receiving "two denarii" for wine, and Abbott-Smith notes its value was close to the Greek drachma, which the denarius gradually replaced.

receipts.how: The landowner agrees to pay workers 'a denarius a day,' directly confirming the definition's identification of the coin as a standard day's wage for a laborer.
Jesus asks for a denarius to examine, illustrating the singular sense and the coin's role as a familiar everyday Roman silver coin.
The plural 'a hundred denarii' owed by a fellow servant confirms the plural sense (44% of occurrences) is simply a grammatical variation with no shift in meaning.

prose.def: An indefinite adverbial particle meaning 'of whatever kind' or 'at any time at all,' adding a generalizing or -soever force to a relative or other expression.
prose.article: δήποτε is a small Greek particle built from δή and ποτέ that broadens whatever word it attaches to, giving the sense "-soever" or "of any kind at all." It is well attested in everyday Koine: papyri like P Lond 904 and P Tebt 381 use phrases such as "for whatever reason" and "in whatever manner." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just once, in John 5:4, in the phrase "with whatever disease" he was afflicted; the Majority Standard Bible's single rendering there is folded into "stirred."
prose.caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only once in the Byzantine text, is absent from the critical text (its John 5:4 verse is disputed), and even the manuscript reading there varies between ᾧ δήποτε and οἵῳ δηποτοῦν.

prose.def: An emphasis particle meaning "surely" or "of course," strengthening a statement as something the speaker and reader both recognize.
prose.article: δήπου is an emphasis particle that adds the sense of "surely" or "of course" to a statement, presenting it as something acknowledged and beyond dispute. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 2:16, where both the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible render it "surely." Abbott-Smith notes it carries the flavor of "we know," appealing to shared understanding, and it is built from the particles δή and πού.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single passage.

prose.def: A preposition meaning 'through,' 'by,' 'because of,' or 'for the sake of,' marking agency, means, or cause — with genitive usually instrumental, with accusative usually causal.
prose.article: διά is one of the busiest little words in the New Testament, appearing 671 times, and its job is to point at how or why something happens — the channel, instrument, or cause. With a genitive it usually means "through" or "by means of" (143 times rendered "through"), while with the accusative it leans toward "because of" or "for the sake of" (51 times "because"). It's so grammatically woven into sentences that in 230 of those 671 cases it gets absorbed into English phrasing without a word of its own, and in the Septuagint it most often stands in for the Hebrew כֵּן ("so, thus," 255 times). Tellingly, διά survived into Modern Greek as γιά, still meaning "for" — as in γιὰ τοῦτο, "therefore."
prose.caution: Its meaning shifts heavily with case and context, so any single rendering is a rough guide, not a fixed equivalent.

The caution note is good but the definition itself does not signal the genitive/accusative case split, which is the single most important usage key for ordinary readers.

prose.def: To cross over from one place to another, used both transitively (crossing a body of water) and intransitively (moving toward a destination), and occasionally of an uncrossable barrier.

to cross over / come over (intransitive, with εἰς or πρός)
prose.article: διαβαίνω means to step across or cross over, often a river, sea, or boundary, built from διά ("through") plus the base meaning "step." In the Greek Old Testament it shows up 118 times, overwhelmingly translating the Hebrew verb עָבַר ("to pass over"), 102 of those times. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, and everyday papyri use it the same way—one document urges someone to "go over to Dionysias and find out," the same construction with εἰς that we see in Acts 16:9.

prose.def: To bring a charge or complaint against someone, ranging from a neutral report to malicious slander or false accusation.
prose.article: In the New Testament διαβάλλω appears only once, in Luke 16:1, where the BSB and Majority Standard Bible both render it "accused." The word literally means "to throw across," and from there it stretches to slandering, defaming, or accusing — though the everyday papyri show it could mean simply "complain of" without any necessary implication of malice or falsehood. One papyrus letter even cautions that the charge in Luke 16:1 need not assume slander, since the verb was used for ordinary complaints.
prose.caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a range running from neutral complaint to malicious slander, the precise force in Luke 16:1 is uncertain.

prose.def: To affirm something emphatically and with solemn insistence, presenting it as firmly established fact.
prose.article: This verb means to affirm or insist on something with confidence, presenting it as certain. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the Pastoral Epistles—once of false teachers who 'confidently assert' things they don't understand (1 Timothy 1:7) and once of Paul telling Titus to keep stressing sound teaching (Titus 3:8). The everyday papyri are revealing: legal documents use it for formally 'confirming' facts in inheritance disputes, such as one person attesting that certain people had died before the mother (BGU I.19), which shows the word's force of solemn, binding assertion.
prose.caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the two listed senses are really one idea (confident assertion) rendered two ways in English rather than a genuinely divided range.

The classical and papyri evidence shows a wider range: lexicons note an older sense "to carry over," and a striking inscription from an Asclepieum describes a god in a blind man's dream using his fingers to "draw apart" the closed eyelids — a literal, physical use far removed from the New Testament's "passing time."
prose.caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and one of those absorbed into a phrase, the measured evidence is thin, so confidence is low.

prose.def: Someone who officially takes over another person's role or position, sometimes with the nuance of a formal court or military title; a successor.
prose.article: διάδοχος means a successor — someone who steps into another person's official role. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 24:27, where Porcius Festus succeeds Felix as governor (the MSB happens to render the surrounding phrase as the name "Porcius"). The most interesting detail comes from the papyri: Deissmann showed that διάδοχος could be a formal court or military title, originally applied to Alexander's reinforcements before it came to mark a particular rank or privilege among his successors.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range cannot be measured from usage alone.

The Septuagint uses it 35 times for Hebrew words like חָצָה ("divide," 12×) and חָלַק ("apportion," 10×), and everyday papyri use it for dividing up land between heirs or parties. In the New Testament it appears only twice: once in 1 Corinthians 12:11, where the Spirit "apportions" gifts to each person, and once in Luke 15:12, where it is absorbed into the phrasing of dividing an inheritance.
prose.caution: With only two New Testament occurrences (one not even rendered by its own English word), confidence in the measured range is low.

prose.def: To cleanse or purge thoroughly, used in the NT specifically of the Messiah clearing a threshing floor by winnowing away chaff.
senseLabels: cleansing/purging thoroughly (with winnowing as the specific NT application)
prose.article: This verb combines "through/thoroughly" with "cleanse," giving the sense of cleaning something out completely. In both of its New Testament appearances (Matthew 3:12 and Luke 3:17) it describes John the Baptist's image of thoroughly clearing the threshing floor, which is why the Majority Standard Bible renders it "winnowing" 100% of the time. A nice everyday parallel survives in a papyrus from about 250 B.C. that uses the related form for a man who "cleaned out" the water-channels in a tent, showing the word's plain practical sense of clearing something out.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin — only 2 occurrences, and the lexica list slightly different forms (διακαθαρίζω in Matthew, διακαθαίρω in Luke), with critical editions favoring the latter spelling.

prose.def: To thoroughly confute or defeat an opponent's argument, as in public debate; used once of Apollos refuting Jewish objections in Corinth.
prose.article: This rare verb describes winning an argument decisively—not just disagreeing, but thoroughly demolishing the other side's case. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 18:28, where Apollos powerfully refutes the Jews in public debate. The word is built from layered prefixes (διά + κατά + ἐλέγχω, 'to refute'), and these stacked intensifiers are what give it the sense of utterly, completely defeating an opponent.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force rests on a single passage and the related verb it is built from.

prose.def: To serve or minister to someone's practical needs, including table service, material support, and (in 1 Tim 3) formal service as a deacon.

The Majority Standard Bible renders it "serve" in 20 of 37 occurrences (69%), with "ministered" and "minister" filling out the rest, and the Berean Standard Bible agrees with every choice. prose.def: Practical service or assistance rendered to others, ranging from domestic tasks to formal religious ministry, financial relief, and official church office.
prose.article: διακονία covers the whole range of serving others, from waiting at a table to the formal work of ministry in the church. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note that this word is almost absent from everyday papyri before the sixth century A.D., suggesting it was somewhat literary or reserved for an almost technical use until it entered common speech.

prose.def: A person who serves others as an attendant or agent, and in some contexts the formal church office of deacon or deaconess.

One striking detail: Moulton-Milligan shows from papyri and inscriptions that the word was already a technical title for the holders of religious and civic offices before Christian times, which paved the way for its later use as the church office of "deacon."

prose.def: The cardinal number two hundred, used to count people, amounts of money, distances, or other quantities, often integrated into surrounding Greek phrasing.
senseLabels: the number two hundred (modifying persons, monetary amounts, distances, or other quantities)
prose.article: This is simply the cardinal number "two hundred," formed from the words for "twice" (δίς) and "hundred" (ἑκατόν). It appears 8 times in the Byzantine New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "hundred" (as part of "two hundred") in 3 cases and folds it into the surrounding phrasing in the other 4. It is far more common in the Septuagint, occurring 78 times across 16 books, where it counts everything from raisins to male goats.
prose.caution: In half of its New Testament occurrences the word is absorbed into English phrasing rather than rendered as a standalone word, though its meaning is not in doubt.

prose.def: To hear someone out fully and judicially, especially of an official or judge giving a prisoner or petitioner a complete formal hearing.

prose.def: To separate and distinguish, judge or decide (active); or, in the middle/passive, to dispute or contend, or to be inwardly divided and so doubt or waver.
senseLabels: to judge, discern, or make a distinction
prose.article: διακρίνω is built from κρίνω ("judge") and διά, giving the core idea of separating things in order to distinguish, evaluate, or decide between them. In the New Testament it stretches across a wide range: in some places it means to discern or make a distinction, in others to judge or settle a matter, and in still others—reflexively—to be split in one's own thinking, hence to doubt or waver. The everyday papyri confirm the practical legal flavor: one document (A.D. 139) uses it for examining tax-collectors, and a third-century B.C. inscription uses it for judges deciding disputed contracts. Notably, the "doubt, hesitate" sense is described as a later Hellenistic development found in the NT but not in the Septuagint, where it instead renders Hebrew words like שָׁפַט ("to judge," 10×).
prose.caution: The measured renderings only capture a fraction of the word's range—4 of 19 occurrences were absorbed into phrasing with no English word, and the lexica list several senses (distinguish, contend, decide) that the counted data barely reflects.

prose.def: To obstinately or forcefully attempt to prevent someone from doing something, with the διά- prefix intensifying the hindrance.
prose.article: This verb means to actively prevent or hinder someone, built from the common word κωλύω ("to hinder") with the prefix διά adding force. prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range in the biblical text cannot be measured.

prose.def: To reconcile—to change enmity into friendship; in its sole NT use, a passive call on one party to make peace with an estranged brother.

prose.def: The scattered community of God's people living among foreigners, or the condition and act of that scattering; applied to Jews and, metaphorically, to Christians.

prose.article: διασπορά describes the scattering of a people far from home, and by extension the dispersed community itself living in foreign lands. It comes from a verb meaning to scatter (like seed broadcast by a sower) and was used especially of Jews exiled and spread across the ancient world; the New Testament writers also apply it metaphorically to Christians (James 1:1, 1 Peter 1:1). In the Septuagint it stands behind several Hebrew words tied to exile and scattering, such as נָדַח and זַעֲוָה, and could even name the exiles themselves rather than the act of scattering.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 New Testament occurrences), and the John 7:35 rendering "intend" reflects translation of the surrounding phrase rather than a distinct meaning of this word itself.

prose.def: To strictly charge, command, or warn someone (middle or passive), often with the force of a binding prohibition or solemn instruction.

The everyday Koine papyri confirm the commanding sense vividly—one letter from 232 BC uses it to mean "give instructions to Ptolemaeus."

prose.def: A measurable gap or interval, whether of time or physical space, between two points or moments.
senseLabels: an interval (here temporal: 'about three hours later')
prose.article: διάστημα names a gap or interval — it can mark a stretch of time or a distance between physical objects. In the New Testament it appears only once, at Acts 5:7, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "later," referring to a span of about three hours that passed. The everyday papyri show both uses vividly: an astronomical document measures the interval of day and night, while a land survey speaks of a ditch and a considerable space between plots, and a Septuagint preface (Sirach) likewise uses it of a time interval.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests almost entirely on Septuagint and papyri evidence.

prose.article: At its root διαστρέφω means to twist or distort, and in the New Testament it works almost entirely in a moral sense: a "perverse" generation, a man "subverting" the nation, leaders who draw disciples "away" after them. senseLabels: bring safely through danger or peril
prose.article: διασώζω means to carry someone safely through some threat — a storm, an illness, an enemy — and deliver them to safety. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 8 times, and the Majority Standard Bible most often captures it simply with "safely" (3 times, half the occurrences), as when Paul is brought safely through shipwreck and journey in Acts. The everyday Koine papyri show the same flavor vividly: one letter rejoices that grain "made it through" safely, and another reports being "brought safely through great dangers," the very sense the word carries in Scripture. In the Septuagint it appears 57 times, frequently rendering the Hebrew מָלַט, "to escape" or "slip away to safety."
prose.caution: Of the 8 occurrences, only 3 produce a distinct English word and 2 are absorbed into phrasing, so the measured sense rests on a fairly small base.

prose.def: A formal arrangement, disposition, or ordinance issued by a recognized authority, including both divine governing decrees and (debated) angelic mediation of the law.
senseLabels: disposition or ordinance (mediated through angels, sense debated)
prose.article: διαταγή refers to something formally arranged or commanded by an authority — an ordinance or institution. It appears only twice in the New Testament, where it covers both the law "ordained" through angels (Acts 7:53) and the governing "ordinance" of God that one must not resist (Romans 13:2). Grimm once claimed this was a purely biblical and church word, but Deissmann overturned that: the papyri show it in ordinary commercial life, such as an order for the payment of wine (P Oxy I.92) and an arrangement for a grape harvest (P Fay 133).
prose.caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence is thin, and the lexicons themselves debate the exact sense in Acts 7:53.

prose.def: A formal edict or commandment issued by someone in authority, such as an emperor, king, or magistrate.
senseLabels: an authoritative edict, commandment, or decree
prose.article: διάταγμα refers to an authoritative edict or decree handed down by someone with power to command. It appears only once in the New Testament (Hebrews 11:23) and twice in the Septuagint, where it once renders a Hebrew word. In Roman times it was the technical term for an imperial edict, and the papyri show it used for the decrees of emperors and prefects \u2014 one document even applies it to a testamentary disposition.
prose.caution: The Byzantine NT rendering recorded here as "parents" looks like a data error, since every lexicon and the papyri agree the word means an edict or decree.

prose.def: To authoritatively order, appoint, or prescribe; used actively, in the middle, and passively (what was commanded or ordained).
prose.article: διατάσσω means to arrange thoroughly or to give authoritative directions, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it 15 times across 6 books. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as "directed" in a third of cases (as in Acts 7:44, 1 Corinthians 16:1, and Titus 1:5), while in 6 of 15 occurrences it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing with no English word of its own. A striking detail comes from the papyri: the verb had a technical legal use in connection with wills, where it meant a sum "bequeathed" — one document records twenty silver drachmae left by a deceased father.
prose.caution: Only one clear measured sense emerged, and 6 of 15 occurrences were absorbed into phrasing, so its full range is hard to pin down from the rendering data alone.

prose.def: To continue or persist in an action, typically expressed with a participle complement indicating what one keeps on doing.
prose.article: διατελέω literally means to accomplish thoroughly, but in practice it works as a verb of persistence — to keep on doing something continuously. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 27:33, where Paul notes that his companions have continued without eating; here the Majority Standard Bible's rendering is tagged "daybreak," reflecting the surrounding clause rather than the verb's core meaning. The everyday Koine papyri capture its flavor nicely: one writer says he has "long administered the revenues with regularity," and another that he is "continually praying to the gods."
prose.caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a measured-sense label ("daybreak") that reflects the context rather than the verb itself, confidence is low and the rendering data should be read cautiously.
